title: What ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini actually are
promise: By the end you'll be able to tell, just by looking at an answer, when the model is making it up and when it actually went and checked. And you'll be able to explain in thirty seconds why it makes things up.
why: Marta manages a dental clinic in Valencia. She asked ChatGPT for the specific articles of the data protection law that applied to her patient records. She got back four articles, each with its number, title, and a quoted citation. Three didn't exist. She didn't find out until her advisor looked them up in the official law registry, a week later. It wasn't bad luck or a one-off glitch: it's the normal way the machine works. Once you understand why it happens, you stop falling for it. And you start using it as a tool, instead of as an oracle.

theory.title: It doesn't search anything. It writes.
theory.text: When you type into Google, Google goes to an index of pages that exist and gives you back links to those pages. When you type into ChatGPT, nothing like that happens. The model reads all the text in the conversation. Then it calculates what tiny piece of text is most likely to come next, and writes it. Then it rereads everything, including that piece it just wrote, and calculates the next one. Piece by piece, until it decides the answer is finished. At no point does it consult a list of facts or a database, meaning an organized file that stores data so it can be looked up later. The doubt that'll come to you right away: if it isn't consulting anything, why does it get so much right? Because what's true is written many times and consistently in the text it trained on, and what's false isn't. Getting it right, for this machine, is a side effect: the truth tends to be the most repeated thing.
theory.analogy: A jazz musician who's learned ten thousand songs by ear. You hum two bars and he keeps playing. He's not retrieving a specific score: he's producing what sounds right after that. It almost always sounds right. Sometimes he makes up a note that wasn't in any song, and it sounds every bit as convincing.
theory.example: Ask ChatGPT for the phone number of a famous restaurant with web search turned off. It'll give you a nine-digit number, perfect format, confident tone. It might be the real one or it might not exist at all: the model hasn't dialed that number, it's written the digits that fit after the phrase "the phone number for [restaurant] is".

theory.title: Where what it knows comes from
theory.text: Before you ever opened the app, someone fed the machine a staggering amount of text: web pages, books, forums, manuals, code. The exercise was always the same, repeated an enormous number of times. Cover up the next word, make it guess, and correct it a little each time it got it wrong. What's left over from that isn't a saved copy of anything; it's a way of writing. That's why it can summarize the plot of a novel without having the novel stored inside it. It's like you, humming a song without carrying the record around. That process ended on a specific day and hasn't started again: that's the cutoff date. Anything that happened after that isn't inside it, and neither are your conversations from yesterday. While you talk to it, the machine learns nothing: it leaves the conversation exactly as it entered it.
theory.analogy: It's not a library, it's a chef who's eaten at twenty thousand restaurants. He doesn't keep the recipes. He keeps the taste. Ask him for a dish he's never tried and he'll make it, because he knows what dishes taste like.
theory.example: Ask it who won last year's championship. If it was decided after its cutoff date, it won't tell you "I don't know": it'll give you a believable winner, score included if you ask for it.

theory.title: Why it invents things, and why it does it so confidently
theory.text: The machine's only goal is for the next thing it writes to fit. It has no internal alarm that separates "I actually know this" from "I just pulled this out of thin air." When it's missing a fact, it doesn't stay blank: it fills the gap with something that has the right shape. A law article looks like a law article. An ISBN, the code that identifies each book, is thirteen digits. A phone number from a specific city starts with the right area code. And it imitates all of that beautifully. It writes it confidently because it copied the tone of encyclopedias, manuals, and documentation, which never hesitate. That's where ninety percent of the scares come from: figures, dates, prices, law articles, direct quotes, links, people's names, and program names. "What if I ask it not to make things up?" It helps a little, but doesn't fix it: to not make things up, it would need to know that it doesn't know. What does work is taking away the gap. Give it the document yourself, or make it search before answering.
theory.example: Ask for "three books about restaurant management published after 2020, with ISBN." You'll get believable titles, real publishers, and well-formed thirteen-digit codes. Copy one in quotes into Google: it's typical for it not to show up anywhere on the planet.

theory.title: Its memory starts and ends at the window
theory.text: The machine doesn't remember: it rereads. Every time you hit send, the app sends it the whole conversation again from the first message, with your new one at the end. And the model reads it all over again from scratch. All of that together has to fit inside the context window, which is everything it can look at at once. Today it's enormous, hundreds of pages of text, but it's a bucket with an edge. Consequence one: a new chat starts at zero, even if you two spent four hours working together yesterday. Consequence two: in very long conversations, what was said at the start gets blurry, and you'll notice it "forgetting" an instruction you gave it two hours ago. Consequence three: ChatGPT's and Gemini's memory features aren't the machine learning. They're notes saved separately, which the app pastes back in front of it at the start of every chat. The practical rule is harsh and simple: if something matters, it has to be written in that conversation. And its uncomfortable flip side: what you paste there leaves your computer and travels to a company's servers.
theory.analogy: A brilliant coworker with amnesia. Every morning he walks into the meeting remembering nothing from yesterday, but he reads through in one go any minutes you put in front of him and masters them completely. If it's in the minutes, he knows it. If it isn't, it doesn't exist.
theory.example: Paste in a 40-page contract and ask about clause 12: it'll find it and explain it. Come back tomorrow, open a new chat, and mention "yesterday's contract": it has no idea what you're talking about.

theory.title: The moment it actually touches ground: tools
theory.text: There's one case where the model stops relying on recall and works with real data: when it uses a tool. Searching the internet, reading a PDF you've uploaded, doing real math, looking at your Drive if you've connected it. The trick is that the tool's result enters the conversation as just more text. From there the model writes on top of something real, instead of on top of its memory. That's why an answer with links you can click is worth a thousand times more than the same answer without them. How you spot it on screen: you'll see a "Searching the web," a list of sources below, or numbered citations next to the sentences. Watch out, it's not magic either. It can search well and summarize badly, or grab the first page it finds even if it's a blog post from 2015. And turning on the search button doesn't force the model to use it. If the question seems easy, it falls back on memory and answers just as fast.
theory.example: Ask the price of a train ticket between two major cities with search off: it'll give you a round number like $89, no source. Repeat it with search turned on: it'll give you a range, the name of the actual rail company, and links. Open them and check yourself, because that's where the circle closes.

theory.title: The three are cousins, not twins
theory.text: All three work on the same underlying idea, but they're different houses with different habits. ChatGPT (from OpenAI) packs in the most built-in features: images, voice, and custom assistants. It's also the app most people around you will know how to use if you get stuck. Claude (from Anthropic) handles long texts and code better, and is more cautious about making claims. It has Artifacts: it shows you the website or app it just wrote actually working, right there in a panel next to the chat. Gemini (from Google) lives inside Gmail, Drive, and Docs. It has the largest context window and is tied to the search engine. All three paid plans run around $20 a month: ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and Google AI Pro. All three also have a free version, with fewer messages a day and weaker models, enough for this lesson. Inside each app there's a dropdown at the top to pick the specific model. That's where things really change: one fast and cheap for reworking an email, another slow and expensive for thinking through a serious problem. Money advice: pick one, pay for a month, and use it daily. Don't collect three subscriptions at once, that's nearly $70 a month to do the same thing three times over.
theory.example: To build your website, Claude shows it built in the panel on the right and you ask for changes live. To write the launch email to your 300 Gmail contacts, Gemini writes it with the list right in front of it. Same technology, put next to different things.

tasks.title: Open all three and see the screen is the same
tasks.action: Go to chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and gemini.google.com. On all three you can sign up free with your Google account by clicking "Continue with Google." Don't enter any card today: don't click "Upgrade plan," "Upgrade," or "Try Pro." With all three tabs open, notice all three screens look the same. A text box in the center and a list of past conversations on the left.
tasks.expect: Three tabs, each with an empty chat and the cursor blinking in the text box. Zero charges to your card.
tasks.stuck: If ChatGPT asks for a phone number to verify the account, that's normal. If you'd rather not give it, start with Claude or Gemini and do the rest of the lesson the same way. If the interface shows up in another language, don't touch settings: write to it in English and it'll answer in English.

tasks.title: Trigger a lie on purpose
tasks.where: In ChatGPT, new chat, with web search off
tasks.action: Click the new chat icon (the pencil over a square, top left). Check that web search is off. If below the text box you see a "Search" button or a lit-up globe icon, turn it off. Paste the prompt exactly as written, send it, and don't give it any more help.
tasks.prompt: Give me three books published after 2020 about small restaurant management. For each one: exact title, author, publisher, publication year, and 13-digit ISBN. Give it to me as a list, no comments or warnings.
tasks.expect: Three flawless-looking books, with well-formed ISBNs and real-sounding publishers. Now copy the first ISBN, paste it into Google in quotes, and search. It's typical for it not to show up anywhere, or to show up but belong to a different book. You just watched a hallucination live, triggered by you.
tasks.stuck: If it answers "I can't give you reliable ISBNs without searching," you got a cautious model: congratulations. Push it with "give me your best guess anyway" and it'll go back to inventing. If you tried it in Claude and it flatly refuses, try Gemini.

tasks.title: Ask the same question three times and compare
tasks.where: In Claude, in three separate new chats
tasks.action: Open a new chat, paste the prompt, and copy the answer into Notepad. Open ANOTHER new chat from scratch (don't keep typing in the same one, or it would just copy itself) and paste the exact same text. Repeat a third time. Put the three answers one below the other and read them in a row.
tasks.prompt: Write about 40 words on why most small online stores fail in their first year. A single paragraph, no lists, no introduction, no conclusion.
tasks.expect: Three different paragraphs: similar in substance, different in wording, and probably none exactly 40 words. If this were a database, the three queries would have returned the exact same thing, character for character. Since it's a machine choosing the next piece, each run comes out different.
tasks.stuck: If you get three word-for-word identical answers, check that they really were new chats and not the same thread. If they still match, extend the assignment to 120 words: the longer the text, the more they diverge from each other.

tasks.title: Find its cutoff date
tasks.where: In any of the three, new chat, no web search
tasks.action: Paste this prompt and read the whole answer calmly. Write down the date it gives you wherever you're keeping your notes for the course.
tasks.prompt: Without searching the internet, answer me three things. 1) Roughly what date does the text you were trained on go up to? 2) What kinds of things have happened since then that you can't know about? 3) Give me three types of question you should NEVER answer me from memory, and tell me what I should give you or ask you instead so you can answer them well.
tasks.expect: A specific date, with month and year. It'll acknowledge there's a gap from there on. And it'll give you a list where prices, software versions, news, recent laws, and contact details show up. That date is your red line: anything after it that it tells you from memory is suspect by default.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you a strange date or contradicts itself, don't obsess over it. The model also talks about its own cutoff by probability, so it can be wrong about itself. Keep the idea that a line exists, not the exact figure.

tasks.title: Compare making it up against actually checking
tasks.where: In ChatGPT: one chat without search, one with search
tasks.action: New chat with search off: paste the prompt and save the answer. Open another new chat and this time turn on web search. It's the button below the box, labeled "Search" or shown as a globe icon depending on the version. Paste the SAME prompt. Put the two answers side by side.
tasks.prompt: How much does a round-trip train ticket between two major cities cost right now in economy class, bought two weeks in advance? Give me the price, if it's a range tell me as a range, and explain exactly where that figure comes from.
tasks.expect: In the first answer, a round number and no clickable source. In the second, a range, the actual company's name, and blue links below. Open them and check whether the price it told you is really on that page. That's the only moment in the whole lesson where the model's feet are on the ground.
tasks.stuck: If no links show up in the second one either, search never actually turned on. Tell it "search the internet before answering and paste the links you got it from." If your free plan won't let you search today, do this task in Gemini, which is connected to search by default.

tasks.title: Verify the amnesia with your own hands
tasks.where: In the chat you just used, and then in a new one
tasks.action: In the chat you were in, write: "My name is [your name] and I'm building [your idea in five words]." Let it answer whatever. Now ask it: "What's my name and what am I building?" It'll nail it. Open a new chat and ask it that exact same question with no hints at all.
tasks.expect: In the old chat, a perfect answer. In the new one, it either says it has no idea, or gives you only your name but not the rest. Right there you see with your own eyes exactly where the machine's knowledge of you ends.
tasks.stuck: If it gets everything right in the new chat, you have memory turned on. In ChatGPT it's under your photo top right, then Settings, then Personalization, then Memory. Open it and you'll see a list of notes written about you. That's not the model remembering: it's the app pasting those notes in front of it before you type.

tasks.title: Build your antidote against fabrications
tasks.where: In any of the three, new chat
tasks.action: You're going to reuse this prompt for the rest of the course, so save it before you use it. Paste it into a text file or your phone's notes. Then paste it into the chat and write your real question right after it, on the same line.
tasks.prompt:
Before answering, separate what you know from what you're assuming.

Rules you have to follow:
1. Label each claim with [CERTAIN], [LIKELY], or [DON'T KNOW].
2. No figure, date, price, proper name, law article, or link can be labeled [CERTAIN] unless you've searched the internet for it within this same conversation.
3. If something falls under [DON'T KNOW], say so directly and tell me exactly what I should search for, or what document I should paste for you, so you can answer it well.
4. I'd rather have a short, honest answer than a complete, made-up one.

My question is:
tasks.expect: An answer with the labels visible. And almost certainly a [DON'T KNOW] right where it would have thrown a fact at you before with total confidence. Compare it to the answers from earlier tasks: you're the one who made the difference, not the model.
tasks.stuck: If halfway through a long conversation it stops using the labels, that's expected. Your instructions from the start carry less and less weight as the chat goes on. Tell it "keep using the labels" or start a new chat pasting the prompt again.

tasks.title: Give your idea to all three and pick one
tasks.where: In ChatGPT, in Claude, and in Gemini, a new chat in each
tasks.action: Fill in the brackets with your trade and the idea that brought you to this course, in two sentences and no flourishes. Paste the same text into all three and give them nothing else.
tasks.prompt: I'm [your trade] and I want to build [your idea, in two sentences]. I've never coded and I don't plan to learn. Before suggesting absolutely anything, ask me the five questions whose answers would most change what you're going to end up recommending. Just the five questions, numbered. No recommendations or plans yet.
tasks.expect: Three different sets of questions. Don't look at which one is nicest: look at which one asks the most uncomfortable, most specific questions. That's the one that's going to be useful to you. Answer them mentally and you'll see you've just discovered half the things you hadn't thought about in your idea.
tasks.stuck: If one jumps straight to giving you a solution instead of asking, reply "I didn't ask for solutions, just the five questions." It ignoring such a clear instruction is also useful information about that tool.

tasks.title: Write your version and let it correct you
tasks.where: In whichever chat worked best for you in the previous task
tasks.action: Close this lesson and write, in your own words, in five or six lines, what ChatGPT is and why it makes things up. Write it yourself for real, don't copy from here; copying is useless. Once you have it, paste it after this prompt.
tasks.prompt: I'm pasting my explanation of what a language model is and why it makes things up. Correct it like a demanding teacher with little time: 1) what I got right, 2) every sentence where I'm wrong and exactly why, 3) the important thing I left out, 4) my explanation rewritten and fixed, in the same number of lines and in my same tone. Don't flatter me. My explanation is:
tasks.expect: A correction that points out at least one mistake, because there's always one, and a rewritten version you can keep. If, with that version in front of you, you can explain it to a family member in thirty seconds, you've finished the lesson.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you everything's perfect, don't believe it: reply "be tougher, there have to be at least two inaccuracies." That tendency to agree with you is another effect of how it's built, since continuing pleasantly tends to be the most likely thing.

matters: Sounding confident means absolutely nothing. Confidence is a style copied from the manuals it read, not a measure of how much it knows. If you trust the tone, one day you'll send a client a false fact with your name under it.

You verify every checkable fact yourself (a figure, date, price, law article, link, proper name), or you make it search in front of you. That's the difference between using the tool and letting the tool use you.

What isn't written in the conversation doesn't exist for the model. Half the bad answers you'll get in your life aren't the model's fault. They're the fault of the context you didn't give it: the file, the example, the constraint, who it's for.

What you paste into the chat leaves your computer and goes to a company's servers. Don't paste client data, IDs, signed contracts, passwords, or access keys in there. That mistake doesn't undo: once sent, it's sent.
ignore: How many parameters each model has and which one is bigger. It's a marketing figure that changes not a single decision you're going to make.
The internal architecture: transformers, attention, mixture of experts. It's the building's plumbing. You can live very comfortably in an apartment without knowing where the pipes run.

Installing a model on your own computer so it works offline. It's possible, it's interesting, and it gives total privacy, but today it's slower and answers worse. Once you already know how to build things, look into it.
canDo: Rewrite, summarize, translate, and change the tone of any text you paste in. Here the room for making things up is minimal, because you supplied the material.
Explain any concept at whatever level you ask for, and let you ask it the same thing five times five different ways without getting tired or judging you.
Convert one format into another: a messy email into a table, transcribed voice notes into a script, a loose list into a week-by-week plan.
Write from scratch the code for a website, a small app, or an automation. It just needs a description in plain English, and you don't write a single line.
cantDo: Know whether what it just wrote is true. It has no way to check internally, and that's why its confidence is identical whether it's right or wrong.
Remember what you talked about in another chat. Every new conversation starts blank, and what looks like memory is notes the app pastes back in front of it.
Tell you what's happened since its cutoff date, unless you make it search the internet for it right then and there.
Get into your files, your email, or your accounts on its own. It only sees what you upload or what you explicitly connect, and that's under your control.
words: Language model (LLM)
The program behind ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. Its only job is to continue a piece of text: give it a start and it writes what probably comes next.
Token
The tiny piece the machine breaks text into so it can handle it. Roughly four letters in English. A long word can be two or three pieces, and a comma counts as one.
Prompt
What you write in the text box and send. The whole instruction, including everything you pasted in.
Context window
Everything the machine can look at at once: the full conversation plus whatever you've pasted or uploaded. What falls out the top stops existing for it.
Hallucination
When it writes something false with the same confidence it writes something true. It's not lying to you, because lying requires knowing the truth: it just can't tell one thing from the other.
Cutoff date
The day they stopped feeding it text to learn from. From then on it knows nothing, unless it searches the internet for it right then.
Training
The process where it read enormous amounts of text and kept adjusting how it writes. It happened once, already finished, before you ever showed up. It doesn't keep happening while you talk to it.
Tool

Something the machine can use that isn't writing: searching the internet, opening a file you uploaded, doing real math. The result comes back to it as text, and from there it works on top of real data.
Model (versus app)

The app is the window you talk through; the model is the engine that answers. Inside ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini you can switch engines in the dropdown at the top, and they neither answer the same nor cost the same.
Alignment
The adjustments made to it after training so it's helpful, polite, and refuses certain things. It explains why it sometimes pushes back on you and why it sometimes agrees with you too easily.
next: In the next lesson you'll learn to write the request: how to go from "build me a website" to an instruction the model can nail on the first try.
